teaser: A tired painter took a break from his big project. The break became his most famous picture.
review_notes:
1836 context: Cole was working on The Course of Empire for Luman Reed, who urged him to paint something for the National Academy of Design exhibition; Reed died in June 1836; Cole married Maria Bartow in November 1836. 'Essay on American Scenery' published January 1836.
Cole's composition relies on his own 1833 sketch and, by most scholars, on a print in Basil Hall's 'Forty Etchings' (1829).
The 'Hebrew letters' on the distant hill (Noah / Shaddai) are a modern scholarly interpretation (Matthew Baigell), presented as such.
The river cut through the neck of the oxbow in a flood of 1840; Interstate 91 now crosses the old loop.
Gift of Mrs. Russell Sage to the Met, 1908. Size about 131 x 193 cm.

lesson.text: By early 1836 Thomas Cole was worn out. He was 35 and deep into The Course of Empire, five large canvases about the rise and ruin of a civilization, ordered by a New York merchant named Luman Reed. The work dragged, his spirits were low, and he had nothing new to show at that spring's big exhibition.

Reed gave him sensible advice: stop for a while and paint something people can buy. Cole agreed to do a landscape, quickly, on a canvas he already had stretched. He chose a view he had sketched three years earlier, from the top of Mount Holyoke in Massachusetts, looking down on a great loop of the Connecticut River.

That year turned Cole's life over. Reed, his patron and friend, died suddenly in June. In November Cole married Maria Bartow and settled for good in the village of Catskill, in the Hudson Valley that had made his name.

Cole had arrived from England as a teenager and fell hard for American wilderness. Painters who followed him are known as the Hudson River School: artists who treated the forests and rivers of the young country as a subject as grand as any ruin in Europe. And in 1836 he was worried about it.

That January he had published an essay praising American scenery and mourning what he called the ravages of the axe. Forests were being cleared at a speed he found shocking. Keep that in mind, because his “quick” landscape is cut into two halves that do not agree.
Cole builds the picture like an argument with two sides.

lines.label: The dividing line
lines.text: From the edge of the storm cloud down the slope of the mountain, one long diagonal splits the canvas. Left of it: dark, wet, wild. Right of it: sun and farmland.

lines.label: The blasted tree
lines.text: A storm-broken trunk leans in from the left edge. Battered trees were Cole's shorthand for untamed nature: nobody has tidied this hillside.

lines.label: The river
lines.text: The Connecticut doubles back on itself before leaving at lower right. A bend this tight is called an oxbow, after the U-shaped collar of an ox yoke.

lesson.text: Many viewers see a question mark in that river, and it suits the picture. The storm is moving off to the left, taking the wilderness with it, or it is on its way back. The valley is tidy, fertile and peaceful, or it is the first chapter of the story he was telling in The Course of Empire. Cole does not say.
The Oxbow is two landscapes in one frame, wild America and settled America, with the painter refusing to tell you which one wins.
He does tell you where he stands, quite literally. Cole put himself in the picture, tiny, at work. He is easy to miss among the rocks and ferns of the foreground.
The painter is sitting somewhere on this mountain with his canvas. Can you find him?

spots.title: Thomas Cole
spots.text: Just a hat, a coat and the edge of an easel between two boulders. He has turned his head to look back at you, as if you had walked up behind him.

lesson.text: His place is telling: on the wild side, at the very edge, facing the farms. A few steps to his right his gear waits on a rock. From there on the picture rewards slow looking, because the “peaceful” valley is full of small signs of people changing the land.

lesson.title: Reading the valley
lesson.text: Three details that sharpen the argument.

spots.title: The umbrella
spots.text: A folded sketching umbrella is planted in the rock beside Cole's bag. It sticks out over the river like a flag, linking the wild half to the tame one.

spots.title: Fields and haystacks
spots.text: Neat rectangles of crops, rows of stacked hay, a small sailboat on the water. Every tree down here has been left standing by someone's decision.

spots.title: The scarred hill
spots.text: Pale clearings have been cut into the forest on the far hill. Some scholars read their shapes as Hebrew letters spelling a name of God. Others see logging scars. Both readings fit Cole.

lesson.text: Cole may have had help from an unlikely source. A British traveler, Basil Hall, had published a print of this exact view after complaining that Americans did not appreciate their own scenery. Cole traced it while in London and seems to have used the outline.

The painting was shown at the National Academy of Design that spring under its full title: View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm. It sold. Cole went back to his five canvases and finished them later that year. The “break” is now better known than the project it interrupted.

At about 1.3 by 1.9 meters (51 by 76 inches) it is a big picture for a side job, and it set a pattern. For decades American painters climbed mountains to paint wide views with a storm on one side and promise on the other. Cole did not see much of it. He died in 1848, at 47.

Nature revised the view four years after Cole painted it. In 1840 a flood pushed the river straight through the narrow neck of the loop, leaving the oxbow as a cut-off lake. Today an interstate highway runs across it.

quiz.question: Why did Cole paint The Oxbow in 1836?
options: He needed something to exhibit while a bigger project dragged on
He had just moved to Massachusetts
quiz.explanation: His patron urged him to pause The Course of Empire and paint a saleable landscape.

quiz.question: What does the left half of the painting show?
quiz.explanation: The left is dark, wet and wild; the right is sunlit farmland.

quiz.question: Where is Cole himself in the picture?
options: In a boat on the river
Among the foreground rocks, at his easel
quiz.explanation: He sits between boulders and looks back at the viewer.

quiz.question: What is an oxbow?
options: A tight U-shaped bend in a river
A farm tool shown in the fields
quiz.explanation: The name comes from the U-shaped collar of an ox yoke.

quiz.question: What had Cole written about earlier that year?
options: The ravages of the axe on American forests
quiz.explanation: His essay on American scenery mourned the rapid clearing of forests.

facts.text: Cole was born in the United States and never left it.
facts.explanation: He arrived from England as a teenager.

facts.text: The loop of river in the painting was later cut off by a flood.
facts.explanation: In 1840 the river broke through the neck of the oxbow.

facts.text: The Oxbow was one of the five canvases of The Course of Empire.
facts.explanation: It was a separate landscape painted during a pause in that series.
